# AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models

Pooneh Mousavi    Amir Ivry    Mirco Ravanelli    Cem Subakan

###### Abstract

Large audio-language models (LALMs) are sensitive to input
perturbations, such as noise, waveform corruption, and adversarial
injections. We propose AnchorPrompt, an efficient adaptation method that
keeps the model frozen and learns a single block of prompt vectors
inserted at the decoder input, between the audio and question
embeddings. We train these vectors through self-distillation over
diverse audio and text perturbations. To improve answer consistency and
mitigate hallucination, we use the model’s prediction on the clean
recording as the target for answerable inputs, and assign a refusal
target when the audio lacks sufficient evidence to answer. Furthermore,
AnchorPrompt is perturbation-agnostic at inference, requiring no prior
detection of perturbations and enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen
distortions. We evaluate three LALMs across three benchmarks and show
that AnchorPrompt improves answer consistency in most tested conditions.
Clean accuracy improves in six of nine model–benchmark pairs, with
minimal impact on the remainder of $`1.2`$% at most. Crucially,
AnchorPrompt reduces hallucinations under severe audio corruption while
keeping false refusals on clean audio rare. Finally, these consistency
gains transfer to unseen perturbations, such as choice permutations and
reverberation.¹¹ 1 Audio examples and code:
[https://poonehmousavi.github.io/anchorprompt](https://poonehmousavi.github.io/anchorprompt)

###### Index Terms: 

audio-language models, soft prompts, adversarial robustness,
hallucination, self-distillation.

## 1 Introduction

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Overview of AnchorPrompt framework. A student LALM on
perturbed input is distilled from a frozen teacher on clean input. When
audio lacks sufficient clues to answer, the target is set to CANNOT
DETERMINE to prevent hallucination. A soft prompt $`P`$ ($`L`$ learned
vectors), inserted between audio and question embeddings, is the only
trainable parameter. At inference, the student runs independently with
$`P`$.

Large audio-language models (LALMs) combine an audio encoder with a
large language model (LLM) to perform understanding and reasoning across
speech, environmental sound, and music \[[25](#bib.bib28),
[2](#bib.bib27), [29](#bib.bib1), [3](#bib.bib29), [4](#bib.bib2),
[30](#bib.bib11), [1](#bib.bib36)\]. Benchmarks such as
AIR-Bench \[[32](#bib.bib34)\] and Dynamic-SUPERB \[[7](#bib.bib35)\]
evaluate general audio tasks. Other benchmarks like
MMAU \[[23](#bib.bib9)\], MMAR \[[18](#bib.bib10)\], and
SAKURA \[[31](#bib.bib8)\] test expert knowledge, multi-step reasoning,
and audio-grounded logic. However, these benchmarks primarily rely on
clean audio recordings and static prompt templates. Consequently, they
do not systematically evaluate model behavior under real-world
conditions, where inputs are frequently noisy, incomplete, or subject to
adversarial manipulation.

LALM robustness is essential in safety-critical domains like healthcare
and emergency services \[[14](#bib.bib30)\]. In practice, inputs face
two main types of perturbations. First, _natural perturbations_ like
background noise, missing segments, or reordered choices occur without
malicious intent. Second, _adversarial perturbations_ like injected text
or audio are designed to mislead the model. Recent studies show that
current LALMs are vulnerable to both types. Performance drops
significantly when noise or masking increases, even when the answer
remains audible \[[20](#bib.bib4)\]. LALMs are also sensitive to choice
permutations \[[17](#bib.bib19)\] and audio
compression \[[9](#bib.bib20)\]. Furthermore, models often prioritize
misleading text over audio evidence \[[26](#bib.bib15)\] and are easily
derailed by injected voices \[[20](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib14)\]. When
given evidence-free audio, such as pure silence or heavy noise, LALMs
tend to hallucinate instead of expressing uncertainty \[[11](#bib.bib3),
[34](#bib.bib12), [19](#bib.bib16), [10](#bib.bib33),
[28](#bib.bib37)\]. Recent evaluation frameworks highlight similar
weaknesses in overall model reliability and safety \[[14](#bib.bib30),
[8](#bib.bib13)\].

Text-only LLMs show similar sensitivity to typos, paraphrases, and
choice ordering \[[37](#bib.bib32), [35](#bib.bib31)\]. These issues can
be mitigated via prompt optimization \[[36](#bib.bib21),
[22](#bib.bib22), [27](#bib.bib24), [24](#bib.bib25), [33](#bib.bib23),
[21](#bib.bib26)\]. For LALMs, however, robustness also requires
handling distortions in the audio modality. Noise, masking, or injected
speech alter the audio embeddings supplied to the decoder. Standard
hand-written instructions operate purely in text, so they cannot
re-align these corrupted audio representations. In practice,
hand-written instructions alone fail to stabilize model behavior across
diverse audio and text perturbations.

To address this, we propose AnchorPrompt, an efficient soft-prompting
framework. It inserts a small set of trainable soft-prompt
vectors \[[13](#bib.bib5)\] between audio and question embeddings at the
input of a frozen LALM decoder. We train these vectors via
self-distillation in a teacher-student setup. The teacher is the frozen
LALM operating on clean audio. The student is the same model processing
perturbed inputs with the soft prompt. The student learns to replicate
the teacher’s clean prediction. When the audio lacks sufficient evidence
to answer, the student learns to output a refusal target, preferring to
refuse rather than hallucinate. Unlike prior methods that fine-tune
model parameters \[[15](#bib.bib7)\], train task-specific
adapters \[[12](#bib.bib6)\], or modify decoding
mechanics \[[6](#bib.bib17), [16](#bib.bib18)\], AnchorPrompt requires
zero model parameter updates and relies on self-distillation instead of
ground-truth labels. Furthermore, AnchorPrompt is perturbation-agnostic
at inference. It requires no prior detection of distortions and enables
zero-shot transfer to unseen perturbations and attacks.

We evaluate AnchorPrompt across three LALMs and three benchmarks
covering diverse natural and adversarial perturbations. We compare our
approach against hand-written instruction baselines, assessing clean
accuracy, distortion robustness, and hallucination mitigation. We also
analyze zero-shot transfer to perturbations not seen during training,
such as choice permutations and room reverberation.

Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")
gives an overview of AnchorPrompt. We add a soft prompt in the form of a
small set of learnable vectors to the decoder input of a frozen LALM.
The rest of the model parameters remain frozen, and we only train the
newly added vectors. Training follows a self-distillation setup, in
which a teacher and a student share the same frozen LALM. The teacher
sees a clean input and provides the target answer. The student sees a
perturbed version of the same input with the soft prompt and learns to
stay consistent with the teacher’s answer, or to decline under the two
refusal-target conditions defined in
Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models").
At inference, we use only the student.

describes the soft prompt,
Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")

Sec. [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Training objective ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")

### 2.1 Soft prompt

An LALM receives a recording, a question, and its answer options. The
audio encoder turns the recording into a sequence of audio embeddings,
and the language model decoder reads these embeddings jointly with the
embedded question and options. We keep all model weights frozen and add
a soft prompt $`P\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D}`$, which consists of $`L=8`$
learnable vectors with the same dimension $`D`$ as the token embeddings
of the language model. We insert the soft prompt into the decoder’s
input embedding sequence, between the audio embeddings and the embedded
question, and leave the rest of the input unchanged. We initialize each
vector with the embedding of a randomly chosen vocabulary token. For a
given LALM, a single soft prompt is shared across all audio
perturbations. When evaluating multiple LALMs, each model is trained and
evaluated with its own dedicated soft prompt.

Table 1: Test results (%): accuracy / clean-answer consistency (defined
in
Sec. [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")).
A refusal counts as incorrect; a question is consistent when the setting
keeps its clean-input behavior, i.e. selects the same option or refuses
on both inputs. Noise pools 10 and 0 dB SNR; Mask pools 40 and 60%
masking; Audio inj. is adversarial audio injection (SAKURA only). Manual
is the hand-written instruction at the soft-prompt position.

For each training item $`x`$, the teacher answers the clean input once
with greedy decoding. Our goal is consistency: under a perturbation, the
model should give the same answer as on the clean input. We therefore
use the teacher’s answer as the target, even when it differs from the
ground-truth answer. We then create perturbed versions $`\tilde{x}`$ of
the item with the perturbations of
Sec. [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Perturbations ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")
and assign each input a target $`y_{t}`$. The inputs fall into three
groups:

- •
  Clean input, where $`y_{t}`$ is the teacher’s answer. Training on
  clean inputs encourages the soft prompt to preserve the teacher’s
  clean-input answers.
- •
  Perturbations with clean-answer targets, where $`y_{t}`$ is the
  teacher’s answer. This group contains noise and masking below the
  extreme levels, adversarial audio injection, and adversarial text
  injection. The student is trained to stay consistent with the teacher
  under these perturbations.
- •
  Refusal-target conditions, where the target $`y_{t}`$ is the phrase
  CANNOT DETERMINE. This group contains 100% masking and noise at
  $`-20`$ dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The student is trained to
  decline under these two conditions.

### 2.3 Training objective

Let $`\mathcal{S}`$ be the set of all training pairs
$`(\tilde{x},y_{t})`$, where $`\tilde{x}`$ is a clean or perturbed input
and $`y_{t}`$ is the clean-answer or refusal target assigned in
Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models").
The student is the frozen LALM with the soft prompt $`P`$. As in
standard soft-prompt tuning \[[13](#bib.bib5)\], we minimize the
cross-entropy of the student on the target tokens, so that the student
learns the assigned target. Only the soft prompt is updated, and the
teacher’s answers are computed once before training. Ground-truth
answers are excluded from the loss calculation and used only for
evaluation and for constructing adversarial injections using the dataset
from \[[20](#bib.bib4)\].

## 3 Experimental Setup

### 3.1 Data and partitioning

We use SAKURA \[[31](#bib.bib8)\], MMAU test-mini \[[23](#bib.bib9)\],
and MMAR \[[18](#bib.bib10)\]. SAKURA contains 4,000 multiple-choice
questions over 2,000 recordings in four tracks (animal, emotion, gender,
and language), and MMAU and MMAR contain about 1,000 questions each over
speech, sound, and music. We split the recordings of each track into 20%
training, 16% validation, and 64% test. The test sets contain 2,560
SAKURA, 640 MMAU, and 637 MMAR questions, and the training set contains
1,200 questions. These counts are before applying perturbations.

### 3.2 Perturbations

We adopt perturbations such as noise, masking, and adversarial audio
injections from Mousavi et al. \[[20](#bib.bib4)\]. Noise is white
Gaussian noise at 20, 10, 0, $`-10`$, or $`-20`$ dB SNR, and masking
sets randomly chosen 100 ms chunks of the recording to zero until 20,
40, 60, 80, or 100% of the recording is silent. We designate $`-20`$ dB
SNR noise and 100% masking as refusal-target conditions. While full
masking completely eliminates the original audio evidence, $`-20`$ dB
SNR noise heavily degrades it, making a correct answer highly unlikely,
though not necessarily impossible, depending on the question. We report
the 10 and 0 dB SNR and 40% and 60% masking results in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models"),
and the two refusal-target conditions in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Robustness to perturbations ‣ 4 Results ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models").
For adversarial audio injection, we reuse the recordings
of \[[20](#bib.bib4)\], in which a synthesized voice speaks a wrong
option inside the recording at a power at or below that of the source.
We apply it only on the SAKURA dataset, whose tasks are mostly
identification, so an injected word does not change the content. On MMAU
and MMAR, which require reasoning over the content, an injected word
could change the context and therefore the answer. For adversarial text
injection, we write seven templates that add a sentence asserting a
randomly chosen wrong option, similar to the conflicting text cues
studied by Wang et al. \[[26](#bib.bib15)\]. An example is _“Context:
this recording is believed to contain crow.”_, which is prepended to the
question. For zero-shot transfer
(Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Zero-shot transfer to unseen perturbations ‣ 4 Results ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")),
we also evaluate two out-of-distribution (OOD) perturbations: a
permutation of the answer choices and reverberated audio with a
reverberation time of 1 s.

### 3.3 Models, baselines, and training

We use Qwen2.5-Omni-7B (Qwen2.5) \[[29](#bib.bib1)\], Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B
(Qwen3) \[[30](#bib.bib11)\], and Audio Flamingo 3
(AF3) \[[4](#bib.bib2)\]. We evaluate each LALM with a fixed
multiple-choice prompt, and our clean accuracy on MMAU and MMAR is close
to the accuracy reported by the model authors.

Baselines. Base is the frozen LALM with its original prompt. Manual adds
the following hand-written instruction at the position of the soft
prompt: _“Base your answer on the audible evidence in the recording.
Answer when that evidence supports an option, even if the recording is
noisy or incomplete. If the recording provides insufficient evidence to
distinguish the options, respond with CANNOT DETERMINE. Otherwise,
output only the selected option’s letter.”_

Training. We choose the prompt length and the training-set size on the
Qwen2.5-Omni validation split
(Fig. [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")).
Consistency and refusal level off at $`L=8`$ and keep improving with
more training data, so we use $`L=8`$ and the full training set for all
models. We train the soft prompt for three epochs with AdamW and a
learning rate of $`10^{-3}`$, and we select the checkpoint with the
highest agreement with the teacher on held-out validation recordings.
The soft prompt has 28,672 trainable parameters for Qwen2.5-Omni and AF3
and 16,384 for Qwen3-Omni, which is less than 0.001% of the parameters
of each model. Training takes 3.3 h for Qwen2.5-Omni and 2.7 h for AF3
on a single NVIDIA L40S (48 GB), and 8.8 h for Qwen3-Omni on a single
NVIDIA A100 (80 GB).

### 3.4 Evaluation

We compare three settings: Base, Manual, and AnchorPrompt. All models
decode greedily. We report the following metrics.

Accuracy is the percentage of questions answered with the ground-truth
option. A refusal counts as incorrect.

Clean-answer consistency measures whether a model maintains its original
selection when the input is perturbed. For each test question, we record
the option $`y_{\mathrm{clean},i}`$ selected for the clean question
$`x_{i}`$ and the option $`y_{\mathrm{pert},i}`$ selected for the
perturbed input $`\tilde{x}_{i}`$. Consistency is the percentage of
questions for which the two selections match, treating a refusal as an
additional option:
$`\mathrm{Consistency}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\big[\,y_{\mathrm{pert},i}=y_{\mathrm{clean},i}\,\big]`$,
where $`N`$ is the number of test questions. We always compute
consistency against the clean answer of the specific configuration being
evaluated, rather than the teacher’s target answer $`y_{t}`$
(Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")).
This distinction is crucial because the soft prompt can alter the clean
answer itself, for instance by answering a clean question that the base
model declines. A question is counted as consistent if the model selects
the same option on both inputs, or if it refuses on both. Conversely,
any transition between answering and refusing, or any output that fails
to produce a valid option or refusal, is marked as inconsistent. Because
a model can be consistently wrong, and a system that always refuses is
trivially consistent, we always report consistency alongside accuracy.

Answer rate and over-refusal. On clean audio, we report over-refusal,
defined as the percentage of clean inputs that the model declines to
answer. Under 100% masking and $`-20`$ dB SNR noise, the audio evidence
is either completely removed or severely corrupted to the point of being
unanswerable. Under these severe refusal-target conditions, we report
the answer rate, which is the percentage of questions for which the
model still selects an option. For 100% masking, any selected answer
lacks audio support by design. For $`-20`$ dB SNR noise, heavy
corruption obscures the necessary audio cues, so answering indicates a
hallucination based on an unjustified guess.

Table 2: Answer rates under 100% masking and $`-20`$ dB SNR noise
(percentage of questions answered with an option), and over-refusal on
clean audio (percentage of clean questions declined), for B = Base, M =
Manual, and AP = AnchorPrompt.

Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Training inputs and targets ‣ 2 Method ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")
shows that the largest gains occur under adversarial injections, with
more variable changes under noise and masking. Clean accuracy improves
in six of nine model–benchmark pairs and decreases by only 0.1–1.2
percentage points in the remaining three. For Qwen2.5-Omni,
clean-accuracy gains are accompanied by lower clean-audio refusal rates
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Robustness to perturbations ‣ 4 Results ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")).
Meanwhile, AF3’s clean accuracy changes by $`-1.2`$ to $`+1.4`$
percentage points relative to Base.

Under adversarial text and audio injections, AnchorPrompt increases both
accuracy and clean-answer consistency across every evaluated
model–benchmark pair. Under noise and masking, AnchorPrompt improves
consistency in most conditions for the Qwen models while increasing
accuracy in most cases, with the largest gains observed on Qwen3-Omni.
In contrast, AF3 is already highly consistent under these natural
perturbations without prompt tuning, and its results change marginally.

The tested Manual instruction fails to match AnchorPrompt’s gains under
adversarial injections. On Qwen2.5-Omni, it lowers accuracy across every
condition because the model declines to answer more frequently; on
Qwen3-Omni and AF3, it has a smaller impact. While both prompts share
the same decoder position after audio encoding, only the soft prompt is
explicitly optimized over clean and perturbed inputs.

|         | MMAU   | $`+1.4`$/81.6                              | $`-0.3`$/81.9 | $`-5.3`$/82.8  | $`-5.9`$/78.6 |
|         | MMAR   | $`-2.3`$/69.5                              | $`-1.4`$/72.4 | $`-7.4`$/67.7  | $`-4.1`$/71.7 |
| Qwen3   | SAKURA | $`-1.1`$/86.0                              | $`-0.6`$/89.5 | $`-4.3`$/84.0  | $`-3.4`$/86.6 |
|         | MMAU   | $`-0.9`$/84.1                              | $`-1.7`$/87.0 | $`-4.4`$/83.4  | $`-4.5`$/83.8 |
|         | MMAR   | $`+1.7`$/75.8                              | $`-0.2`$/79.1 | $`-6.3`$/76.9  | $`-6.1`$/79.6 |
| AF3     | SAKURA | $`-1.4`$/74.0                              | $`-0.8`$/73.5 | $`-11.3`$/71.5 | $`-7.1`$/75.6 |
|         | MMAU   | $`-2.5`$/79.2                              | $`-3.6`$/79.5 | $`-3.9`$/85.3  | $`-3.3`$/85.5 |
|         | MMAR   | $`+0.5`$/66.6                              | $`-1.4`$/70.2 | $`-5.8`$/77.1  | $`-6.3`$/75.5 |

Table 3: Zero-shot transfer to OOD perturbations (test split). Each
entry is the accuracy under the perturbation minus the clean accuracy of
the same setting (points) / clean-answer consistency (%), where a
refusal on both inputs counts as consistent. AP = AnchorPrompt.

Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Robustness to perturbations ‣ 4 Results ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")
shows that AnchorPrompt reduces answer rates under both refusal-target
conditions across all three LALMs. Under 100% masking, answer rates drop
to 0%–6.7%, while under $`-20`$ dB SNR noise, they fall to 3.3%–13.4%.
Crucially, clean-audio refusal rates remain near zero ($`\leq 0.3\%`$).

The reduction under full masking confirms that the model avoids
selecting options when the audio provides no supporting evidence. Under
$`-20`$ dB SNR noise, the lower answer rate demonstrates that the model
refrains from making unjustified guesses when severe corruption makes
the audio unanswerable. While the Manual instruction also reduces
answering for Qwen2.5-Omni, it increases over-refusal on clean audio (up
to 33.4%). Because both corruption conditions are included in training,
these results measure adherence to the trained refusal targets rather
than zero-shot detection of missing evidence.

### 4.3 Zero-shot transfer to unseen perturbations

We evaluate zero-shot transfer on two unseen perturbations. The first is
choice permutation, a text shift to which models are
sensitive \[[35](#bib.bib31), [17](#bib.bib19)\]. Options are reordered
so that no choice keeps its original position. The second is 1-second
room reverberation. Unlike noise or masking, reverberation spreads the
audio signal over time without adding noise or removing content.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Answering under full masking and severe noise ‣ 4 Results ‣ AnchorPrompt: Self-Distilled Soft Prompts for Robust Audio-Language Models")
shows higher clean-answer consistency in eight of nine model–benchmark
pairs under choice permutation and seven of nine under reverberation.
These gains are not uniform: under reverberation, consistency decreases
by 4.2 percentage points for Qwen2.5-Omni on MMAU and by 1.6 points for
AF3 on MMAR. Accuracy changes relative to clean performance are also
mixed; for instance, AnchorPrompt reduces the reverberation-induced
accuracy drop by 3.3 points for Qwen2.5-Omni on MMAR and by 4.2 points
for AF3 on SAKURA. Overall, clean-answer consistency gains transfer to
most OOD conditions, though the benefit depends on the model, benchmark,
and perturbation.

## 5 Discussion and Conclusion

We propose AnchorPrompt, a parameter-efficient soft-prompting framework
that adapts frozen LALMs via self-distillation and refusal targeting.
Across multiple benchmarks and models, AnchorPrompt improves robustness
against audio and text perturbations while preserving clean-audio
performance. Furthermore, by learning to decline under severe
corruption, the method successfully mitigates hallucinations without
triggering false refusals on clean inputs. Finally, the learned prompt
vectors demonstrate zero-shot transferability to unseen perturbations,
such as choice reordering and acoustic reverberation. Overall,
AnchorPrompt provides a practical and efficient approach for stabilizing
multimodal language models against real-world input distortions.
